title: The One Where Ross Hugs Rachel

jokes.text: Want to hear something weird? Always. I didn't get the annulment. We're still married.
jokes.setup: Ross asks if Phoebe wants to hear something weird; she says 'Always' — implying she's heard plenty of Ross's nonsense before
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals he never got the annulment and is still married to Rachel
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's 'Always' is a perfect character beat — it acknowledges the absurdity of Ross's life without breaking the scene. The cold drop of the revelation is well-paced. Strong cold-open energy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: There's something I need to tell you.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my god, what? Tell me!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm still married.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What?!

jokes.text: Don't tell Rachel. See you later.
jokes.setup: Ross has just revealed he's secretly still married to Rachel and that it's a huge problem
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to 'Don't tell Rachel. See you later.' — breezy and dismissive as if he's solved it
jokes.explanation: The economy here is excellent — Ross's entire self-delusion is captured in four words and a cheerful exit. Classic Ross avoidance behavior rendered as comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What?! You got married?!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, and we're having a baby. Oh, and I quit my job at the museum.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: WHAT?!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Anyway, I should probably get going. See you later.

jokes.text: Oh, but we'll be late for the movie. Oh, there's a cab. Taxi! Oh, that's great. What timing! My God, huh? There you go. We're gonna walk. It's right at the Angelika. Oh, the Angelika! Go! Go!
jokes.setup: Phoebe tries to pull Ross aside to talk about the annulment secret; Ross and the others are desperate to leave before she can tell Rachel
jokes.punchline: The group generates increasingly frantic excuses — a conveniently appearing cab, the Angelika reference — to escape before Phoebe can say anything
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — the audience sees Ross panic and everyone conveniently disappear. Gets laughs from the situation but the specific lines aren't particularly sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, get in the cab! Get in the cab!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Just get in the cab!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, what is going on?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No time to explain! Walk! Walk! No, wait, get back in the cab!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Make up your mind!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The cab! Yes, the cab! Go, go, go!

jokes.text: "Three divorces! Three divorces!"
jokes.setup: Ross explains why he didn't get the annulment — he went to his lawyer's office but couldn't go through with it
jokes.punchline: He imitates the voice in his head screaming 'Three divorces! Three divorces!' — revealing his real motivation is vanity and shame, not love
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific. Ross performing his own internal shame spiral — the repetition doubles down perfectly. The audience recognizes this as quintessential Ross neurosis. Strong character integration score.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So I'm at the lawyer's office, and the receptionist is talking about me in this really judgmental tone...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, a high voice! That's the universal voice of judgment.

jokes.text: I just don't want my tombstone to read 'Ross Geller: Three Divorces.'
jokes.setup: Ross is spiraling about the shame of a third divorce
jokes.punchline: He's already imagining his tombstone and the specific wording — catastrophizing in peak Ross fashion
jokes.explanation: The tombstone image is a perfect absurdist escalation of Ross's catastrophizing. Specific enough to be funny, bleak enough to be interesting. Sets up the next joke beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Why don't you just put 'Here lies Ross Geller, he never got divorced.' That way when you die, it'll be ironic.

jokes.text: Don't worry about that. Your tombstone can say whatever you want.
jokes.setup: Ross laments that his tombstone will say 'Three Divorces'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe responds with sincere, literal reassurance that he can write whatever he wants on his tombstone — completely missing the emotional point
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe logic — she takes the metaphor literally and offers entirely practical comfort that misses the emotional point entirely. High character integration because only Phoebe would say this sincerely. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! I want mine to say, 'Phoebe Buffay: She had fun, she had friends, she had fun, she had friends.'

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's very nice.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, actually, on second thought, just put 'Phoebe Buffay,' and then... 'Trampled by ostriches.'

jokes.text: It can say, 'Ross Geller: Good at Marriage.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just said the tombstone can say whatever he wants
jokes.punchline: She helpfully suggests the most ironic possible alternative — 'Good at Marriage' — delivered presumably with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The irony lands because Phoebe may genuinely mean it as encouragement, which makes it funnier than a straight sarcastic delivery would be. Excellent economy — four words do enormous work.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I can keep a secret. I'm very good at keeping secrets. I have secrets I haven't even told myself.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, what? Oh my God, no, I have to tell Rachel! She's my best friend!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But... you're right, I do know something that nobody else knows. I'm like special. I'm like the only one. Okay, I won't tell her.

jokes.text: You know? Mine's gonna say, 'Phoebe Buffay: Buried Alive.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is discussing what tombstones can say, trying to comfort Ross
jokes.punchline: She casually reveals her own tombstone plan is 'Buried Alive' — implying this is both a fear and perhaps a legal instruction she's left
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. It's perfectly Phoebe — dark, specific, absurd, and delivered as if this is the most natural thing in the world. 'Buried Alive' works on multiple levels: is it a fear? A protest? A warning to gravediggers? The ambiguity is what makes it brilliant. High quotability — this is the kind of line fans repeat. Genuinely exceptional character integration; no other character on any other show would say this.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, what are you doing? I have to go!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh, I'm sorry. I thought you were... someone else.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Someone else? Phoebe, you were literally blocking the door.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know, I know. Weird mix-up.

jokes.text: Okay, stop, stop! Phoebe? Hey, Rach! What was that? Sorry. Mix-up. How was the movie? I haven't seen it yet. You'd better hurry. The Angelika! Go. Go! No!
jokes.setup: Phoebe nearly blurts the secret to Rachel; everyone scrambles to redirect
jokes.punchline: Phoebe calls it a 'mix-up' and then Ross desperately deploys the 'Angelika! Go! Go!' line again to hurry Rachel away
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'Angelika! Go! Go!' is a minor running gag that gets a mild laugh from repetition. The 'mix-up' brush-off is functional but thin. The cringe of the near-miss lands adequately.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: The Angelika! The Angelika!

jokes.text: Phoebe almost immediately spills to Rachel — 'Hey, Rach!' — and then has to cover: 'Sorry. Mix-up.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe just agreed to keep Ross's secret; Rachel immediately appears
jokes.punchline: Phoebe instinctively calls out to Rachel with the energy of someone about to share gossip, then has to awkwardly abort with 'Sorry. Mix-up.'
jokes.explanation: Quick physical-ish comedy beat. Phoebe can't even maintain the secret for 30 seconds. 'Mix-up' is a wonderfully insufficient cover. Works as both character comedy and a quick laugh, though it's fairly low-stakes.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, Joey won't let us have a gumball machine? Joey, who eats everything?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I have very strict rules about sweets.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you once ate an entire box of girl scout cookies that were supposed to be for charity.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Those were thin mints! That's different!

jokes.text: When we move in together, can I get a gumball machine? Of course. Joey wouldn't let you have one? No, when it comes to sweets, he's surprisingly strict.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are discussing moving in together
jokes.punchline: Chandler reveals Joey is 'surprisingly strict' when it comes to sweets — a completely unexpected and oddly specific character detail for Joey
jokes.explanation: The joke works because 'surprisingly strict' is such an unexpected qualifier for Joey — a man defined by his appetite. The specificity ('sweets' in particular) makes it funnier than a generic Joey-is-childish joke. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, I need to tell you something. I'm moving out.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I... Monica and I are getting a place together and... I just think it's time for me to...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Chandler, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what, I gotta use the bathroom. I'll be right back.

jokes.text: No, I keep trying. And I can get out 'Joey, I have to...' Then I lose my nerve and I finish with '...go to the bathroom.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks if Chandler has told Joey he's moving out
jokes.punchline: Chandler reveals he keeps chickening out mid-sentence and pivoting to 'go to the bathroom' — showing his inability to have difficult conversations
jokes.explanation: The setup trails off and the punchline ('go to the bathroom') is perfectly anticlimactic. The structure mimics what Chandler actually does — the joke performs the cowardice it describes. Strong character integration because Chandler's conflict-avoidance is a defining trait.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, you gotta see a doctor. That's like, not normal.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm fine, I just like to keep moving.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, but every five minutes? That's either a medical thing or you're just messing with us.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not messing with you!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well something's wrong then. My grandpa had that. They had to remove something.

jokes.text: He may think I'm sick.
jokes.setup: Chandler has been telling Joey 'I have to go to the bathroom' repeatedly instead of breaking the news
jokes.punchline: He dryly notes the unintended consequence: Joey probably thinks he has a medical problem
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. Five words that earn big laughs through pure understatement. The deadpan delivery of a ridiculous but logical consequence is Chandler at his best.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm telling everyone today, and that's final.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, ma'am. Whatever you say.

jokes.text: That's how it'll work now? You'll just order me around? Pretty much. All right.
jokes.setup: Monica tells Chandler they just need to get it over with and tell people
jokes.punchline: Chandler mock-protests her giving orders; Monica confirms 'Pretty much'; Chandler accepts this immediately with 'All right.'
jokes.explanation: A quick, competent joke about the Monica-Chandler power dynamic. Monica's 'Pretty much' is sharp; Chandler's instant capitulation is true to character. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I have something serious to tell you.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're pregnant!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No! No, I'm not pregnant!

jokes.text: You're pregnant! No! No? No!
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler sit Joey down to tell him important news
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately leaps to 'You're pregnant!' — this is the second time this episode someone has assumed pregnancy from a 'big news' setup (first was Phoebe to Ross at 05:14)
jokes.explanation: The 'you're pregnant' guess is a running sitcom trope, but Joey's earnest enthusiasm and the triple 'No' exchange make it work. It's not innovative but it's well-executed for what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, that's great! That's really great for you, man. I'm so happy for you.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, I gotta go.

jokes.text: Joey stares in silence for several beats after learning Chandler is moving out, then abruptly says 'Oh, uh, hey! I'm really happy for you guys. Congratulations. See you later.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just been told Chandler is moving out — a devastating emotional blow for him
jokes.punchline: After a long stunned silence, he goes full denial mode with unconvincing cheerfulness and bolts
jokes.explanation: The humor is in Joey's transparent emotional suppression — his 'happiness' is clearly devastation in disguise. The beat of silence before the forced cheer is what makes this land. Strong character integration; Joey's emotional transparency is his defining quality, so the failed suppression is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'd love to stay, but I have an audition.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Actually, no I don't.

jokes.text: I gotta go. I've got an acting job. Like you'd believe that.
jokes.setup: Joey claims he has to leave because of an 'acting job'
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts his own excuse with 'Like you'd believe that' — self-aware about his career struggles
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-deprecating awareness of his own failed acting career, deployed in the middle of emotional avoidance, is a great double joke. The economy is excellent — the second line does all the work. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Maybe you guys should break up now and get it over with.

jokes.text: Look, if you're gonna move in with him, I feel it is my responsibility to tell you the truth about him. He's a terrible roommate. Terrible. He, uh, forgets to, um... He always, he always, uh... Who am I kidding? He's the best roommate!
jokes.setup: Joey pulls Monica aside, apparently about to dish on Chandler's bad roommate habits
jokes.punchline: He builds up the premise, stumbles on specifics, and collapses into genuine admission that Chandler is the best roommate — revealing his love through his inability to fake criticism
jokes.explanation: This is the emotional peak of the Joey subplot and it works as both comedy and character. The structure — setup, stumble, collapse — is beautifully timed. The joke is that Joey's love for Chandler is so genuine he literally cannot manufacture a complaint. High craft because it earns both a laugh and an 'aw' simultaneously. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Monica, listen, Chandler's a great guy, but...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, he's... okay, he's really funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And he's always there for his friends.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Plus he's got a good job, he's loyal, he's smart...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Actually, he's one of the best guys I know.

jokes.text: You're pregnant. No! Chandler and I are moving in together. Oh, that's good! But if you were pregnant, what would you name it? Hint, Phoebe.
jokes.setup: Monica has exciting news for Phoebe; Phoebe's first guess is pregnancy
jokes.punchline: After being told the real news, Phoebe immediately pivots to what she would have named the baby — with a heavy hint that the name is Phoebe
jokes.explanation: The pregnancy-guess running gag gets its second payoff, but Phoebe's 'Hint, Phoebe' pivot is what elevates this above Joey's version — she's already moved on to baby names and the 'hint' is so baldly self-serving it's delightful.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I found an article about this!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's right here in Ross Geller Magazine.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Ross Geller Magazine?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, it comes out monthly.

jokes.text: Big day, huh? People moving in. People getting annulled.
jokes.setup: Ross is at Monica's after the big news; he makes a casual observation about the day's events
jokes.punchline: 'People getting annulled' — said breezily, though he has NOT gotten the annulment and is still secretly married to Rachel
jokes.explanation: Ross's casual lie embedded in a breezy observation — the audience knows he's wrong, which creates dramatic irony. Good economy; the contrast between 'people moving in' (happening) and 'people getting annulled' (not happening) is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, I have something to tell you.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're pregnant!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, I'm not pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Not yet.

jokes.text: If you see her, give her some really bad news, so mine doesn't seem so bad.
jokes.setup: Ross is heading to find Rachel to tell her about the annulment situation
jokes.punchline: He casually asks Phoebe to pre-traumatize Rachel with worse news so his confession lands softer
jokes.explanation: A solid joke that reveals Ross's selfish coping mechanisms under pressure. The dark logic (cushion my bad news with worse news) is funny because it's so casually monstrous.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not pregnant!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: But if I were, we'd name her Phoebe.

jokes.text: Phoebe alone muttering: 'Bad news for Rachel. What could that be?'
jokes.setup: Ross has just asked Phoebe to deliver bad news to Rachel; Phoebe is left alone thinking about it
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's confused muttering implies she's seriously trying to come up with something — taking the absurd request at face value
jokes.explanation: Phoebe earnestly trying to generate bad news is a good character beat, but it's a reaction laugh rather than a constructed joke. Works as a quick button.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So Monica and Chandler are moving in together. That's great! They're taking this really big step in their relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: They're shacking up!

jokes.text: My life is an embarrassment. I should just go live under somebody's stairs.
jokes.setup: Ross is spiraling about his three divorces and dating prospects
jokes.punchline: 'Go live under somebody's stairs' — a bizarrely specific form of shame-based exile
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'under somebody's stairs' (not a cardboard box, not a bridge) is what elevates this. It's a strangely precise image of shame. Solid absurdist escalation of his self-pity.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, so we're getting the annulment papers filed tomorrow...

jokes.text: The only guys below me will be Four-Divorce Guy, Murderer Guy, and geologists.
jokes.setup: Ross says he's at the bottom of the dating barrel with three divorces
jokes.punchline: He lists the guys below him: Four-Divorce Guy, Murderer Guy... and geologists — a self-deprecating profession joke that undercuts his entire argument
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best Ross jokes in the series. The structure is perfect: escalating list (four divorces → murder) that you expect to end seriously, then 'geologists' as the final entry — which is Ross's own profession. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) it's absurd to rank geologists with murderers, (2) Ross is too self-absorbed to realize he's insulted himself, (3) it reveals his real insecurity isn't just the divorces, it's his whole identity. Comparable to the 9.5 anchor in terms of character specificity and quotability. Genuinely exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Phoebe, could you do me a favor? I need you to find Rachel and tell her something terrible happened.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Tell her that... that a meteor is heading toward Earth and we're all going to die.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Why would I do that?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Because then when you tell her I slept with someone else, it won't seem so bad.

jokes.text: Hi. My friend Ross is about to be divorced for the third time. But wouldn't you date him? And if you wait right here, I'll go get Ross.
jokes.setup: Phoebe decides to prove to Ross that people don't care about his divorces by surveying strangers
jokes.punchline: She asks a random woman on the street to date Ross, then tells her to wait while she fetches him — treating a human being like a blind date appointment she's setting up in real time
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's complete social obliviousness is well-deployed here. The gag of asking a stranger to wait for a date she's setting up cold is a nice absurdist beat. Sets up the more rewarding street interview sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm going to end up living under the stairs like a house elf.

jokes.text: Agh. Thought you were Rachel. What gave me away?
jokes.setup: Ross is hiding from Rachel and jumps when someone approaches
jokes.punchline: Chandler's dry 'What gave me away?' — implying Ross's radar for avoiding Rachel is comically miscalibrated
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean exchange. Chandler's deadpan is well-deployed; the joke is obvious but efficiently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I've hit the bottom of the dating barrel. I mean, I'm dating women with four divorces. Then I dated a murderer. And now... I'm dating a geologist.

jokes.text: [IN DEEP VOICE] Are you scared? Are you? No. [IN NORMAL VOICE] That was my scariest voice. You're brave.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica acknowledge there's no turning back from moving in together
jokes.punchline: Chandler switches to a cartoonishly deep 'scary voice' to ask if Monica is scared, then compliments her bravery for not reacting
jokes.explanation: A charming bit of physical/vocal comedy that plays on Chandler's nervous goofiness. 'You're brave' is a sweet button. Works primarily as performance-dependent humor.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so I've been thinking about how to present you to potential dates.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh God, why does that sound ominous?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, no, it's good! I'm going to lead with your worst quality right away.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, what? That's your strategy?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes! That way, when they don't run screaming, everything else will be a pleasant surprise!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, what is my worst quality?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh honey, we don't have that much time.

jokes.text: You're finally making progress at work, then your boss calls you Racquel. First four years of my work, they called me [BABBLING].
jokes.setup: Rachel is venting about a terrible day at work
jokes.punchline: Her boss called her 'Racquel'; she then tries to describe how they used to mispronounce her name and can only produce babbling sounds — the name was apparently incomprehensible
jokes.explanation: The babbling is a performance-dependent visual gag. 'Racquel' is a solid workplace observation joke. Neither element is particularly sharp in writing but the babbling presumably gets laughs from Jennifer Aniston's delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know what you mean. People always make fun of my name too. At least your name doesn't sound like a—

jokes.text: So everyone's calling me Racquel. By the end of the day, the mailroom guys were calling me Rocky.
jokes.setup: Rachel's boss mispronounced her name as 'Racquel' and no one corrected her
jokes.punchline: The name degraded further through the company hierarchy until the mailroom was calling her 'Rocky'
jokes.explanation: The escalation from Rachel → Racquel → Rocky is a nicely structured comedic degradation. The mailroom detail is specific and grounding. Good economy in the reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: They keep calling me Racquel at work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Then it became Raquel.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Now the mailroom guys just call me Rocky.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm one mispronunciation away from being a boxer.

jokes.text: Well, I still think you're very, very nice and very pretty. What? All yours, babe.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just finished venting; Chandler offers an absurdly inadequate response
jokes.punchline: His patronizing non-sequitur ('very nice and very pretty') is so wrong-headed that Monica immediately hands off the conversation — 'All yours, babe'
jokes.explanation: A quick two-beat joke about Chandler's social incompetence. Monica's 'All yours, babe' is sharp — she's immediately distancing from his terrible response. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: Hey beautiful, you come with the apartment?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Excuse me?

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: I'm looking to rent. Do you come with it?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what? She's not... she doesn't...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't come with anything!

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: Well, that's a deal-breaker then.

jokes.text: The three of us are gonna have such a good time living together!
jokes.setup: Monica has just told Rachel she and Chandler are moving in together
jokes.punchline: Rachel completely misunderstands and thinks she's included — 'The three of us are gonna have such a good time living together!'
jokes.explanation: The misunderstanding is a classic sitcom beat but it's well-executed — Rachel's enthusiasm makes the pending correction more painful and funny. The cringe is effective because we see Monica's face fall.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So we're all moving in together, right? You, me, Phoebe, Joey, Chandler, and Ross?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well... yes and no.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yes and no? Monica, that makes no sense.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know. It's just... okay, yes. We're all moving in together.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yay! This is going to be so much fun!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah... fun. That's one word for it.

jokes.text: Chandler, you'll have to watch those long showers you take, because you know Racquel can't be late.
jokes.setup: Rachel has inserted herself into the living arrangement and is already managing logistics
jokes.punchline: She calls herself 'Racquel' — having accepted the new workplace nickname — while completely missing that she's not moving in
jokes.explanation: A nice callback to the Racquel storyline woven into the misunderstanding gag. The double-layered comedy (she's wrong about living there AND calling herself Racquel) works efficiently.

jokes.text: Rachel gasps and sings 'Come and knock on our door / We'll be waiting for you'
jokes.setup: Rachel is thrilled about the imaginary three-way living arrangement
jokes.punchline: She spontaneously breaks into the Three's Company theme song — a perfect cultural reference for the three-person living situation
jokes.explanation: The Three's Company reference is pitch-perfect for the situation and the era (1999). Rachel's genuine joy makes the pending revelation more cringe-inducing. Good pop culture deployment that earns its use.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Come and knock on our door, we've been waiting for you, come and knock on our door...

jokes.text: First marriage: Wife's hidden sexuality. Not my fault. Second marriage: Said the wrong name at the altar. A little my fault. Third marriage: They shouldn't let you get married when you're drunk and have writing on your face. Nevada's fault.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to rehabilitate Ross's image for the strangers she's recruited to evaluate him
jokes.punchline: Ross's escalating self-defense: 'not my fault → a little my fault → Nevada's fault' — the diminishing personal responsibility with each marriage is the joke
jokes.explanation: Brilliant structured comedy — the three-part list has perfect escalating blame assignment. 'Not my fault → a little my fault → Nevada's fault' is a masterclass in comedic list construction. The 'writing on your face' callback to the Vegas episode is excellent continuity. 'Nevada's fault' is the ideal punchline. This is high-quality sitcom writing comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: My first wife was a lesbian. My second wife cheated on me. And my third wife... well, we got divorced in Nevada, so really, you gotta blame Nevada.

jokes.text: The divorces don't bother me. I'd date him. But not while he's still married.
jokes.setup: Street woman says she'd date Ross despite three divorces
jokes.punchline: 'But not while he's still married' — she doesn't know he actually IS still married to Rachel
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony (she unknowingly describes his exact situation) is the main engine here. Well-structured and the timing of the revelation is sharp. Character integration is low because she's a one-off character.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm a catch! I'm a paleontologist, I have a great apartment, I'm funny...

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: You seem really great, but I heard you've been married three times.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but that was in the past. I'm over all of that now.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: I could look past that... but what about the secret marriage you're hiding?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What secret marriage? I've told you about all of them!

jokes.text: I was only dating guys that were bad for me. So I decided that until I work that... Good. Good. Whatever.
jokes.setup: Street woman starts explaining why she's not dating anyone — a lengthy personal therapy-style explanation
jokes.punchline: Phoebe abruptly cuts her off with 'Good. Good. Whatever.' — having lost patience mid-revelation
jokes.explanation: Phoebe dismissing someone else's emotional processing is funny given she's usually the most emotionally verbose character on the show. The reversal works well.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: I wouldn't date Ross because he's obsessed with his ex-wife.

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: Yeah, no kidding. That's the first thing anyone notices about him.

jokes.text: Well, I don't care about the divorces either. But I wouldn't date him. It's just that he's obviously still in love with this Rachel girl.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to get street endorsements for Ross's datability
jokes.punchline: A complete stranger observes that Ross is 'obviously still in love with this Rachel girl' — an outsider immediately seeing what Ross denies
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the irony that a stranger can see the central will-they-won't-they dynamic more clearly than the characters themselves. It's the show commenting on itself through an outside voice — a form of meta-comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, I don't have feelings for Rachel anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? So if Rachel walked in right now—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I wouldn't care. She's just... she's just my wife.

jokes.text: She said, 'He's obviously still in love with this Rachel girl.' [Ross reacts in shock]
jokes.setup: Ross didn't hear what Meg said and asks Phoebe to repeat it
jokes.punchline: Phoebe repeats it verbatim and directly — no softening, no editing — leaving the brutal assessment hanging in the air
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's unapologetic repetition is funny because she has no impulse to spare Ross's feelings. The reaction beat is the real comedy here — Ross's face is presumably priceless.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I was drunk! I got married in Vegas!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hey, Joey could totally do that sober.

jokes.text: And I have loved her in the past, but now she is just my wife.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to argue he doesn't love Rachel anymore
jokes.punchline: 'She is just my wife' — said as a dismissive correction, without realizing how absurd it sounds
jokes.explanation: Ross says this as a diminishment but the audience recognizes it's the opposite — 'just my wife' is a ridiculous defense. The line encapsulates his self-delusion perfectly. High character integration because only Ross could say this with a straight face.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's amazing! You're like a genius! Yes, yes, exactly! That's so true about Ross!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: *claps* Bravo! Bravo! That was beautiful!

jokes.text: We were drunk! I would've married Joey with that amount of alcohol.
jokes.setup: Ross insists the Vegas marriage was purely a function of drunkenness
jokes.punchline: He specifies he was so drunk he would've married Joey — an extreme example that accidentally sounds affectionate
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke — Joey as the extreme comparator works well. The audience knows Joey is nearby which adds tension to the callback.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't care about Rachel! I'm completely over her. In fact, I'm going to go out with someone else right now. Someone way better!

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: Um... okay?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You're beautiful! We're getting married! I'm naming our children after you!

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: I think you have feelings for someone else.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: NO! I'M FINE! I'M GREAT! I'M THE BEST I'VE EVER BEEN!

jokes.text: Hey! You could do a lot worse than Joey Tribbiani!
jokes.setup: Ross says he would've married Joey drunk — not knowing Joey is nearby
jokes.punchline: Joey overhears and defends himself with genuine indignation — 'You could do a lot worse than Joey Tribbiani!'
jokes.explanation: Joey referring to himself in third person while defending his marriageability is a great character beat. The indignation that Ross wouldn't want to marry him is perfectly Joey — his ego is wounded by what should be an obvious non-insult. High impact because it's a surprise entrance and a crowd-pleaser.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, you're being really creepy about Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I think it's sweet. I like a man who watches me sleep.

jokes.text: Yes, and now he's using this three-divorces reason because he wants to stay married to her because he loves her. I must say, well done. Bravo, Meg.
jokes.setup: Meg the stranger has just laid out the psychological subtext of Ross's behavior
jokes.punchline: Phoebe addresses Meg directly and applauds her analysis — 'Well done. Bravo, Meg.' — as if Meg has just delivered a lecture
jokes.explanation: Phoebe breaking to compliment a stranger's psychological analysis is a funny beat. 'Bravo, Meg' is a nicely absurd touch — Phoebe treating the street encounter like a seminar.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know, I think friendship is the most important thing in life.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? Because yesterday you said you'd abandon all your friends for a rent-controlled apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I mean... that's different! A rent-controlled apartment is... I was joking! Obviously I was joking.

jokes.text: She means nothing to me. Noth... Nothing!
jokes.setup: Ross trying to prove he doesn't love Rachel by committing to getting the annulment
jokes.punchline: He over-protests — 'She means nothing to me. Noth... Nothing!' — the stumble and repetition revealing the opposite of what he claims
jokes.explanation: Classic 'doth protest too much' comedy. The stutter on 'Noth...' is the tell. Well-understood character beat even if the concept is familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Are you pregnant?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? No! Why would you think that?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You've been acting weird all day.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not pregnant. I just really like this shirt.

jokes.text: Okay, now I wouldn't date you because you seem a little creepy.
jokes.setup: Ross over-protests that Rachel means nothing to him
jokes.punchline: Meg, who moments ago offered to date him, withdraws her interest because his vehemence is alarming
jokes.explanation: A good callback — Meg was the one potential date, now she's rescinding. The reversal is clean and the word 'creepy' is perfectly chosen. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, you guys live together? Like, in the same apartment?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes, Rachel. We've lived together for years.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God. I thought... I mean, I just assumed... Oh God, that's so embarrassing.

jokes.text: I am so attracted to him right now.
jokes.setup: Ross has just had his dating prospects tank further due to his overprotesting
jokes.punchline: Phoebe announces she's attracted to him in this moment — finding his emotional mess somehow appealing
jokes.explanation: A quick, punchy button on the whole street-interview sequence. Phoebe's attraction to Ross's worst moment is a funny character beat — her unpredictability is on full display.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait a minute... if this soap has been here since we moved in, and we still have half a bottle left... this stuff must be incredibly concentrated.

jokes.text: Joey's my best friend. I'm not your best friend? You just said...! Ugh. Of course, you're my best friend.
jokes.setup: Chandler reveals he considers Joey his best friend, not Monica
jokes.punchline: Monica's indignant reaction forces Chandler to backtrack immediately, but the damage is done
jokes.explanation: A quick couples' bickering joke. Functional but familiar — the 'partner vs. best friend' tension is a well-worn sitcom beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This apartment won't exist anymore. No more Joey's place. No more 'Hey, let's go to Joey's!' No more of Chandler coming home to find me on the couch in my underwear eating cereal. No more of Monica organizing my stuff that I don't even know I have. No more of Rachel asking to borrow something and never giving it back. No more of Ross explaining something nobody asked him to explain. No more of Phoebe just... being here. And worst of all, no more of me being me in this place!

jokes.text: Oh, yes. Hey, hey. They're not for you. Are you upset? I am now.
jokes.setup: Monica appears with cookies, apparently to soften some news for Rachel; Chandler reaches for one
jokes.punchline: Monica snaps 'They're not for you'; Chandler's 'I am now' — he's been made upset by the denial of a cookie
jokes.explanation: A quick two-beat exchange. 'I am now' is Chandler's reliable deadpan applied to petty cookie denial. Efficient and consistent with his character.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We have deep talks all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Like, just the other day, she asked me what my name was.

jokes.text: Are you pregnant? No, but I'm throwing this shirt away.
jokes.setup: Ross has stopped Rachel to tell her something important; she asks 'Are you pregnant?'
jokes.punchline: Ross says no, then — apparently catching a glimpse of his own shirt — announces he's throwing it away
jokes.explanation: The pregnancy-guess running gag completes its trilogy with an unexpected twist — Rachel asks Ross if HE is pregnant (gender inversion of the gag), and his non-sequitur about the shirt is a visual gag that gets big laughs. The shirt detail is the kind of physical comedy that plays perfectly in multi-cam. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what IS that?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't know, but it's moving.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Don't touch it!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I wasn't planning on it.

jokes.text: When I said that Chandler and I wanted to live together... we meant alone together.
jokes.setup: Monica has to correct Rachel's misunderstanding that she's part of the new living arrangement
jokes.punchline: 'We meant alone together' — the gentle corporate-speak of 'alone together' is a beautifully awkward construction
jokes.explanation: 'Alone together' is a funny oxymoron — the precision of Monica trying to be kind while being clear creates an unintentionally absurd phrase. Good cringe setup for Rachel's reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel didn't even cry about it!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wow, that's... that's a really twisted thing to be upset about.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. That's funny. I can't believe I did that. [LAUGHS]
jokes.setup: Rachel has just been told she misunderstood and is not moving in with Monica and Chandler
jokes.punchline: Instead of showing hurt, she laughs it off — which Monica finds more upsetting than tears would have been
jokes.explanation: Rachel's laughter is both a defense mechanism and the setup for the Monica subplot (Monica wanting emotional validation). The beat works better structurally than it does as a standalone laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: J-Man and Channy? Who actually uses these nicknames?

jokes.text: No more Joey and Chan's. No more J and C's. Want to go to Joey and Chandler's? Can't. It's not there.
jokes.setup: Joey and Chandler are mourning the end of their roommate era
jokes.punchline: Joey role-plays future conversations where someone suggests going to their apartment — 'Can't. It's not there.' — mourning its non-existence with elaborate grief
jokes.explanation: Joey's elaborate grief role-play for a place that will literally still exist across the hall is funny. 'Can't. It's not there.' has a nice absurdist ring to it.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Your second marriage in two years?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Third.

jokes.text: We won't be able in the night and have those long talks about our feelings and the future. Not once did we do that.
jokes.setup: Joey lists things they won't be able to do when they don't live together
jokes.punchline: Chandler flatly corrects him — 'Not once did we do that' — puncturing Joey's sentimentalized version of their friendship
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical. Joey's sentimentalized mythologizing of their friendship (feelings talks, the future) is exactly what two guy roommates would never do, and Chandler's flat correction 'Not once did we do that' is the ideal deadpan deflation. High character integration — both characters are essential to making this land.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: In my twenty years of practice, I've never seen anything like this.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: You're my first client to come back for a second divorce.

jokes.text: And you're upset because you didn't make your best friend cry?
jokes.setup: Monica reveals she's bothered that Rachel didn't cry or get emotional when told she was moving out
jokes.punchline: Chandler reduces her grievance to its absurd core: she's upset she DIDN'T make her friend cry
jokes.explanation: Chandler's ability to reduce irrational emotional arguments to their absurd literal form is a core character skill, and this is a great example. The sentence structure — the 'you're upset because' construction — is perfect for the deadpan style.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: You know, Ross, I think you should consider therapy. You have a pattern of behavior that might benefit from professional help.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Therapy? No, no, I'm fine. I don't need therapy. That's like... that's like ordering the soup when you know the entrée is coming.

jokes.text: All I'm asking for is a little emotion. Is that too much to ask after six years? What, are Rachel and I not as close as you guys? I mean, did we not have as much fun? Don't I deserve a few tears?
jokes.setup: Monica is demanding emotional validation from Rachel's reaction to the news
jokes.punchline: Her escalating demands become increasingly absurd — she wants a specific, quantified emotional response ('a few tears') as validation of their friendship
jokes.explanation: Classic Monica neurosis — she needs external validation of her emotional significance. 'Don't I deserve a few tears?' is funny because it quantifies and demands grief. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We need Rachel to sign the annulment papers.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I could... I could dress up like her and sign the papers myself.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's illegal.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah... yeah, you're right. Maybe I should talk to a therapist about this.

jokes.text: When we told Joey, he cried his eyes out. Hey! I did not cry my eyes out!
jokes.setup: Monica uses Joey's reaction as the benchmark for the emotional response she deserved
jokes.punchline: Joey denies it with indignation — but the fact that he shows up immediately to defend this suggests it's true
jokes.explanation: Joey's denial is funny because his earlier reaction was so transparent. The callback lands well as a callback. The timing of his entrance to defend his dignity is good physical comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, whose is this?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I have no idea. It's not mine.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well it's not mine either.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Maybe it was here when you moved in?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I've lived here for like ten years, Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So... what do we do with it?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I guess we just... throw it out?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay.

jokes.text: Come on, it's like the end of an era. No more J-Man and Channy's! Okay, I gotta ask, who calls us that?
jokes.setup: Joey is riffing on names for their friendship/apartment
jokes.punchline: Chandler asks 'who calls us that?' — J-Man and Channy's being a name Joey apparently invented just now
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean joke. 'J-Man and Channy's' is an inherently funny name, and Chandler's confused 'who calls us that?' is the ideal deadpan response. The affectionate absurdity of Joey's nickname invention is very in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Six years? That's not an era.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Six years is totally an era! That's like, a whole era of my life!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, it's just six years.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Just six years?! Those were MY six years, Rachel! Do you know how much has happened to me in six years?

jokes.text: You got married again?
jokes.setup: Ross has gone back to his divorce attorney to try to get an annulment
jokes.punchline: The lawyer's flat 'You got married again?' — delivered with the exhausted resignation of someone who has seen too much of Ross
jokes.explanation: The lawyer's four-word reaction conveys an entire character dynamic. The economy is near-perfect — maximum exhaustion per syllable. The implied relationship history between Ross and this lawyer is funny without needing to be explained.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not upset. Look, Monica and Chandler have a great track record. They've been together for like five years and they're still happy. That's basically forever in relationship years.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Five years is forever?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: For you guys, yeah.

jokes.text: I have been a divorce attorney for 23 years and never have I had so much business from one client.
jokes.setup: Ross confirms this is his third marriage in two years
jokes.punchline: The lawyer notes the unprecedented volume of business one client has generated — a dry professional assessment that doubles as a devastating personal critique
jokes.explanation: The professional framing ('so much business from one client') is what makes this land — it's clinical and devastating at the same time. The 23-year credential makes the comparison more damning. Well-constructed and delivered with great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, no. This is... this is really happening, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, sweetie. It is.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't believe... I thought maybe... but it's actually...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm really upset now.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, is this the same Rachel whose name you said at the altar in the second marriage?
jokes.setup: Ross explains the Vegas marriage involved Rachel
jokes.punchline: The lawyer connects the dots — same Rachel from the second divorce's infamous wrong-name incident
jokes.explanation: A series-level callback that rewards loyal viewers. The lawyer's incredulous 'is this the same Rachel' makes the pattern explicit and funny. The dry delivery of a stunning coincidence is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I went to see a lawyer about the divorce.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're in love with a lawyer!

jokes.text: Yes, yes, yes. Heh. But I do not love her. Oh. That's better then.
jokes.setup: Ross confirms it's the same Rachel and insists he doesn't love her
jokes.punchline: The lawyer's 'That's better then' — delivered with no inflection, treating this as genuinely reassuring information despite the absurdity
jokes.explanation: The lawyer's deadpan acceptance of Ross's assurance is funny because it's so obviously not 'better then' — it's equally insane. The dry three-word response is excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'll tell her! I'll tell Rachel right now that we need to get an annulment.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you are so in love with her.

jokes.text: Have you considered therapy?
jokes.setup: Ross has explained the Vegas drunken marriage situation
jokes.punchline: The lawyer, whose job is legal advice, pivots to recommending therapy — suggesting the legal system is ill-equipped for Ross
jokes.explanation: Four words that say everything. The lawyer's professional recommendation that Ross seek mental health help is the ultimate deadpan insult, and it's perfectly timed. Near-perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know, everyone always ends up hooking up eventually.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, we will too.

jokes.text: I think just the annulment for today.
jokes.setup: The lawyer has suggested therapy
jokes.punchline: Ross declines with the casual phrasing of someone ordering coffee — 'just the annulment for today'
jokes.explanation: 'Just the annulment for today' has the cadence of a customer service transaction, which is funny because it treats legal proceedings and therapy as equivalent menu items. Ross's obliviousness to his own need for therapy is perfectly captured.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, so in like five years, Chandler's gonna be really rich, and then he's gonna get married, and then divorced.

jokes.text: There's no way to do this without her? Because I kind of already told her it was taken care of. Of course you did.
jokes.setup: Ross learns he needs Rachel present to get the annulment and reveals he already lied to her about it
jokes.punchline: 'Of course you did.' — the lawyer's resigned, unsurprised acceptance of Ross's self-sabotage
jokes.explanation: 'Of course you did' is three words that communicate an entire relationship between this lawyer and his most exhausting client. The resignation in the delivery is key. This lawyer character is doing excellent deadpan work throughout the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So I'm thinking, why don't we just get married?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Really? You want to marry me?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I mean, we could get your green card situation figured out, split the tax benefits, and then in like five years, we just... dissolve it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Joey, that's the most romantic thing you've ever said to me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So is that a yes?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's a 'we'll see.'

jokes.text: What about someone who looks like Rachel?
jokes.setup: Ross learns the annulment requires Rachel's physical presence and participation
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks if a Rachel lookalike would suffice — a legally and logically absurd solution
jokes.explanation: Ross's desperate absurdist solution — a Rachel lookalike for legal proceedings — is perfectly in character. It reveals the depth of his desire to avoid the conversation with Rachel without revealing why. Good originality because it's a specifically ridiculous workaround.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! I got it! We tell them Rachel has a drinking problem!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, no!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? It's perfect! They'll never give her custody!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's... that's not how custody works. And that's horrible.

jokes.text: I will think about the therapy.
jokes.setup: Ross asks if a Rachel lookalike could substitute in legal proceedings
jokes.punchline: The lawyer's response to this insanity is not a legal answer but a renewed commitment to the therapy suggestion
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback structure — the therapy suggestion returns and lands harder because the new context (lookalike request) is more insane than what prompted it originally. 'I will think about the therapy' has perfect deadpan rhythm. Near the top of the lawyer scene jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So what's the plan with Ross?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, we'll probably just murder him after an argument or something.

jokes.text: I don't know if I want it because it might be too many memories. What is that? I don't know.
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel are dividing up their shared belongings
jokes.punchline: Rachel agonizes over an item for sentimental reasons — but neither of them knows what the object actually is
jokes.explanation: A great absurdist beat — the sentimental attachment to an unidentifiable object satirizes the irrationality of moving-related sentimentality. The fact that neither woman knows what it is makes Rachel's attachment even funnier.

jokes.text: Something to remember me by.
jokes.setup: Monica gives Rachel a large plate as a parting gift
jokes.punchline: 'Something to remember me by' — said as if Monica is dying rather than moving across the hall
jokes.explanation: Monica's death-adjacent language for a cross-hall move is funny character work. The irony of 'remember me by' for someone who will literally be 15 feet away is well-deployed.

jokes.text: Mon, you're not dying. I'm just moving out.
jokes.setup: Monica has just said 'something to remember me by' about a plate
jokes.punchline: Rachel correctly identifies the death-adjacent framing and corrects it
jokes.explanation: A clean, efficient button on Monica's melodrama. The line is functionally funny but not exceptional — it's the obvious response delivered well.

jokes.text: Are you okay? You're not blinking.
jokes.setup: Monica has just said it's 'the end of an era'; Rachel doesn't respond emotionally
jokes.punchline: Rachel notices Monica has stopped blinking — a physical manifestation of her suppressed emotional crisis
jokes.explanation: A good visual/physical comedy beat — Monica frozen and unblinking is a funny image. Works better in performance than on the page.

jokes.text: But I gotta say, I don't think six years counts as an era. An era is defined as a significant period of time. It was significant for me. Maybe it wasn't significant to you!
jokes.setup: Monica describes Rachel moving out as 'the end of an era'
jokes.punchline: Rachel pushes back with a literal dictionary definition of 'era'; Monica weaponizes the correction against Rachel
jokes.explanation: A quick spat where the word 'era' becomes a flashpoint for the larger emotional stakes. Monica turning Rachel's pedantry into a personal accusation is funny and in-character.

jokes.text: But I gotta say, I don't think six years counts as an era. An era is defined as a significant period of time. / It was significant for me. Maybe it wasn't significant to you!
jokes.setup: Monica has called their time together 'the end of an era'; Rachel initially plays along then challenges the word
jokes.punchline: Rachel gives a pedantic definition of 'era' and questions whether six years qualifies; Monica takes personal offense at Rachel's definitional objection
jokes.explanation: Rachel suddenly becoming pedantic about the word 'era' is funny — she's unknowingly walked into a semantic trap that Monica turns emotional. The escalation from vocabulary debate to hurt feelings is a good Rachel-Monica dynamic joke.

jokes.text: You were gonna get married in Vegas, and then you backed out. I'm not upset because I don't see you going through with it. I'm sorry.
jokes.setup: Rachel explains why she wasn't more emotional about Monica and Chandler moving in together
jokes.punchline: She admits she didn't believe they'd actually do it — a reasonable but tactless position that undercuts the moment
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the honesty — Rachel accidentally reveals she thinks Monica and Chandler are flaky, which is both insulting and kind of fair. Character-grounded humor.

jokes.text: You were gonna get married in Vegas, and then you backed out.
jokes.setup: Rachel explains why she doesn't believe Monica and Chandler are actually moving in together
jokes.punchline: She references the Vegas almost-marriage — which is ironic given that she herself just had a drunken Vegas wedding
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is rich — Rachel citing Monica's near-Vegas-wedding as evidence of flakiness, while Rachel herself actually went through with a Vegas wedding. The audience has the full picture; Rachel doesn't. Well-integrated with the episode's central secret.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. I'm gonna miss you so much. I'm gonna miss you. I mean, it's the end of an era! I know!
jokes.setup: Monica has finally convinced Rachel it's really happening; Rachel now fully processes the emotional weight
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately adopts Monica's exact language — 'the end of an era!' — now that she actually believes it, as both women erupt in tears
jokes.explanation: The 'end of an era' callback pays off — Rachel using the exact phrase she dismissed is a sweet and funny reversal. The dual crying is a good emotional-comedic beat.

jokes.text: I couldn't. Because you love Rachel. It's not that. Annulments are more complicated — Complicated because of the love.
jokes.setup: Ross returns, having not gotten the annulment again; Phoebe has been convinced he loves Rachel
jokes.punchline: Every explanation Ross gives, Phoebe reinterprets as evidence of love — a closed loop from which he cannot escape
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's immovable certainty about Ross's love creates a funny closed system — whatever he says becomes evidence. 'Complicated because of the love' is a good specific construction.

jokes.text: I do not love Rachel. I'm telling her about the whole thing so we can get this marriage annulled as fast as possible. Would I do that if I loved her? I've never been more convinced of your love for her.
jokes.setup: Ross argues his willingness to tell Rachel and rush the annulment proves he doesn't love her
jokes.punchline: Phoebe interprets his urgency to tell Rachel as further proof of love — 'I've never been more convinced'
jokes.explanation: 'I've never been more convinced of your love for her' is a great Phoebe line — the more he protests, the more certain she becomes. The structure of the exchange is well-designed: Ross's argument inadvertently confirms what he's denying.

jokes.text: Would I do that if I loved her? / I've never been more convinced of your love for her.
jokes.setup: Ross says he's going to tell Rachel everything and get the annulment ASAP — as proof he doesn't love her
jokes.punchline: Phoebe interprets his urgency to annul as further proof of love: 'I've never been more convinced'
jokes.explanation: The joke is that everything Ross does confirms Phoebe's theory — his resistance confirms it, his urgency confirms it, his denial confirms it. 'I've never been more convinced' is a great line because it's paradoxical: his attempt to disprove it is the proof.

jokes.text: Ross hugs Rachel when she's upset — the hug that the episode title references
jokes.setup: Rachel is upset about having to move out; Ross, who is secretly her husband, comforts her
jokes.punchline: The irony of her secret husband hugging her while she doesn't know they're married — the titular moment played as both sweet and absurd
jokes.explanation: The titular moment works as dramatic irony rather than explicit comedy — the audience knows something Rachel doesn't. It earns its rewatch bonus for the layered meaning on second viewing. Impact is moderate because it plays more sweet than funny.

jokes.text: So Ross and Rachel got married. Monica and Chandler almost got married. You think you and I should hook up?
jokes.setup: Phoebe observes the romantic reshuffling happening around them
jokes.punchline: She proposes that she and Joey hook up, by process of elimination/peer pressure
jokes.explanation: A charming and logical absurdist proposal — Phoebe's reasoning (everyone else is coupling up, we're left) is hilariously practical. Sets up the elaborate fantasy sequence to come.

jokes.text: Oh, we do. Ha, ha. But not just yet. Really? Well, when? Okay. Um. Ahem.
jokes.setup: Joey immediately agrees they'll hook up 'but not just yet'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe calls his bluff by asking 'when?' — and Joey has no answer
jokes.explanation: A quick bit of Phoebe-Joey banter. Joey's 'but not just yet' implies a non-existent plan, and Phoebe's immediate 'when?' exposes it. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Well, first Chandler and Monica will get married and be filthy rich, by the way. But it won't work out. Wow. I know. Then I'm gonna marry Chandler for the money. And you'll marry Rachel and have the beautiful kids. Great. But then we ditch those two and we get married. We'll have Chandler's money and Rachel's kids.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is explaining her timeline for when she and Joey will get together
jokes.punchline: She has mapped out an elaborate multi-decade scheme involving marrying Chandler for money and Joey marrying Rachel, then ditching both to run off together — delivered as if this is a perfectly reasonable plan
jokes.explanation: One of the best Phoebe speeches in the episode. The escalating scheme — marry for money, acquire children, then ditch everyone — is delivered with complete sincerity and internal logic. 'We'll have Chandler's money and Rachel's kids' is a great specific punchline. High character integration because only Phoebe would have this fully developed alternative future planned. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in terms of genuine comedic craft.

jokes.text: Then I'm gonna marry Chandler for the money. And you'll marry Rachel and have the beautiful kids.
jokes.setup: Phoebe continues her future-mapping
jokes.punchline: Her plan to marry Chandler 'for the money' — a purely mercenary motive stated with complete honesty
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's unapologetic mercenary motive is funny precisely because she states it without shame. The pairing of her gold-digging with Joey's romantic destiny ('beautiful kids') creates a funny contrast in what each of them gets out of these marriages.

jokes.text: Getting custody will be easy because of Rachel's drinking problem.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has described a scheme where Joey will have Rachel's kids
jokes.punchline: She helpfully explains that custody will be easy to obtain due to 'Rachel's drinking problem' — a completely invented character flaw deployed as a legal strategy
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Rachel's drinking problem' — delivered as a matter-of-fact detail in an already absurd plan — is a perfect escalation. The specificity of using a fake flaw as a legal custody strategy is brilliantly dark. This is Phoebe at her most sublimely unhinged. The economy is excellent; it's a dependent clause that does enormous comedic work. Approaches the quality of the top anchor examples.

jokes.text: Ooh, ooh, what about Ross? I don't want to go into the whole thing, but, um... we have words and I kill him.
jokes.setup: Joey asks where Ross fits into Phoebe's elaborate multi-year scheme
jokes.punchline: 'We have words and I kill him.' — Phoebe casually dismisses Ross's fate in this timeline with casual murder, delivered as a minor inconvenient detail she doesn't want to get into
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best cold-close jokes in Friends history. The escalation from elaborate romantic scheming to 'we have words and I kill him' is perfectly constructed. The understatement — 'I don't want to go into the whole thing' — does phenomenal work, implying there's a whole story she's glossing over. 'We have words and I kill him' is the ideal deadpan for murder as a footnote. The economy is near-perfect. This is genuinely exceptional writing, comparable to the 9.5 anchor example in structure and character specificity. Phoebe casually planning murder is funny because it's inconceivable but also somehow totally in character.

tmdb_overview: Monica and Chandler decide to move in together, leading Rachel to believe that all three of them will be roommates, and Monica doesn't want to tell her the truth.  Meanwhile, Ross tries to keep Rachel from learning that their marriage hasn't been annulled.
insight: Moderate laugh density carries a mid-tier episode leaning on character quirks over setup-payoff structure.
